section.title: Two theorems about continuous functions
section.p: Continuity began as a local condition:
section.md: x\text{ close to }a \quad \Longrightarrow \quad f(x)\text{ close to }f(a).
section.p: But local calm forces global behavior. If a continuous graph starts below a horizontal line and ends above it, it must cross that line somewhere. If a continuous graph lives on a closed finite interval, it must reach a highest point and a lowest point.
These facts sound obvious from a picture. Their hypotheses are where the mathematics lives.

subsection.title: Intermediate values
subsection.p: Suppose the temperature outside is 50^\circF at sunrise and 74^\circF at noon. If the temperature changes continuously, then at some time between sunrise and noon it must have been 60^\circF.
It cannot move from 50 to 74 without passing through the values in between.
The same idea solves equations.

subsection.title: Bisection as a constructive proof idea
subsection.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem says a solution exists. Bisection shows how to trap one.
Return to p(x)=x^3-x-1. We know p(1)\lt 0 and p(2)\gt 0.
Start with the interval [1,2]. Cut it in half. The midpoint is 1.5. Compute:
So a sign change occurs on [1,1.5], because p(1)\lt 0 and p(1.5)\gt 0.
Cut again. The midpoint of [1,1.5] is 1.25. Compute:
So a sign change occurs on [1.25,1.5].
Continuing this process traps a root in smaller and smaller intervals.
After each step, the interval is half as long as before. The intervals are nested:
The Nested Interval Principle traps one real number c in all these intervals. Continuity then forces p(c)=0.

Idea of the proof of the Intermediate Value Theorem. For a target value N, apply bisection to h(x)=f(x)-N. If h(a) and h(b) have opposite signs, repeatedly keep the half interval where the sign change remains. The nested intervals shrink to a point c. Continuity prevents h(c) from being positive or negative, so h(c)=0. Therefore f(c)=N.
This proof idea shows why the real line matters. Bisection produces smaller and smaller intervals. The real numbers guarantee that the intervals trap an actual point.
What the theorem does not say. The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees existence, not a formula. It tells us a root exists in (1,2), but it does not tell us the exact root.
Bisection gives approximations. If we keep cutting long enough, we can make the interval around the root as short as desired. This is one of the first reliable numerical methods in calculus.

subsection.title: Highest and lowest values
subsection.p: Continuity also gives a second global promise.
Suppose h(t) gives the height of a hiker above sea level at time t, for 0\le t\le 4. If h is continuous, then during those four hours the hiker reaches a highest elevation and a lowest elevation.
The hiker cannot have a least upper bound of heights that is approached but never reached, as long as the time interval includes its endpoints and is finite.

subsection.p: The number f(d) is the absolute maximum value. The number f(c) is the absolute minimum value.
The theorem does not say where the maximum and minimum occur. They may occur at interior points, at endpoints, or at several points.

We do not yet have the derivative tools to find them efficiently. But we already know they exist.
This is how the theorem will be used later. Before optimizing a continuous function on a closed interval, we know that the best and worst values are really there.

subsection.title: Why closed and bounded intervals matter
subsection.p: The Extreme Value Theorem has two interval hypotheses: [a,b] is closed and [a,b] is bounded. Both matter.

If the interval is not closed. Consider f(x)=x on the open interval (0,1). The values of f get close to 1, but never equal 1, because x=1 is not in the interval. So f has no absolute maximum on (0,1). The values also get close to 0, but never equal 0, because x=0 is not in the interval. So f has no absolute minimum on (0,1). The missing endpoints matter.

If the interval is not bounded. Consider f(x)=x on the whole real line (-\infty,\infty). There is no largest value and no smallest value. The function can grow as large as we like and as negative as we like. The function is continuous, but the interval is unbounded. The conclusion fails.
If the function is not continuous. Even on a closed bounded interval, discontinuity can break the conclusion. Define
The domain is the closed interval [0,1], but K is not continuous at 1. The values of K(x) get close to 1 as x\to 1^-, but K(x) never equals 1. Also, K(1)=0. So K has no absolute maximum on [0,1].

subsection.title: Why these two theorems matter
subsection.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem and the Extreme Value Theorem do not usually compute answers. They guarantee that answers exist.

example.title: A maximum exists before we know how to find it

statement.p: Suppose a continuous function A(x) gives the area of a rectangle built from a fixed amount of fencing, where x is one side length and 0\le x\le L. Since the possible side lengths form a closed interval and A is continuous, the Extreme Value Theorem says that the largest possible area exists.
Later, derivatives will tell us where it occurs. The theorem tells us that the search is not chasing a ghost.
Some theorems do not calculate the desired number. They tell us the desired number is real and reachable. That is often the first step in solving a problem.

subsection.p: Continuity gave us two promises: no skipped intermediate values, and actual highest and lowest values on closed finite intervals. The next section gathers the warning examples in one place. The goal is to learn when these promises are legal to use, and when a graph is quietly breaking one of the hypotheses.
